content:
Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte will go on trial at the International Criminal Court on Monday, November 30, facing charges of crimes against humanity over thousands of killings carried out during his anti-drug campaign. It will be the first time a former Asian leader has stood trial before the Hague-based court, and the opening day will be watched closely in Manila, where the families of victims have waited almost a decade for a courtroom reckoning.

The trial opens at 10 a.m. in The Hague before Trial Chamber III, composed of judges Joanna Korner, Keebong Paek and Nicolas Guillou. On the first day, the judges will verify that Duterte understands the charges and ask him to enter a plea. Prosecutors will then present their opening arguments, followed by lawyers representing the victims. Duterte, 81, was arrested by Philippine authorities in March 2025 and surrendered to the court. His lawyers have told the judges that he denies the charges.

The charges cover murder and attempted murder allegedly committed between November 2011 and March 2019, spanning Duterte's years as mayor of Davao City and the early years of his presidency. Prosecutors have named 85 murders and two attempted murders in the case, but they say those victims are only a sample of as many as 30,000 people killed by death squads and police operations targeting users and sellers of illegal drugs. If convicted on any of the three counts of crimes against humanity, Duterte could face life in prison.

The scale of the killing is one of the most contested facts in the case, and the gap between the official count and independent estimates is itself part of the story. Philippine law enforcement agencies acknowledged 6,248 deaths during anti-drug operations under Duterte. United Nations agencies, the Philippine Commission on Human Rights, the country's Supreme Court and domestic human rights groups put the number of killings by police and unidentified assailants at between 20,000 and 30,000. Prosecutors allege the killings were carried out as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians, and that Duterte created, funded and armed the death squads behind them.

More than 500 alleged victims will be represented in the proceedings through common legal representatives, who will present their views to the court. The prosecution plans to call about 100 witnesses, with the first five expected to testify before the court's winter recess. The trial is expected to run well into 2027. Under the Rome Statute, Duterte is presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt, and he retains the right to challenge the prosecution's evidence and present his own witnesses.

For the families, the opening of the trial is the moment they have been working towards since the killings began. Llore Pasco, a mother who lost her two sons in the drug war, is travelling to The Hague to attend the proceedings. The trial will open on her 73rd birthday. "My only wish is not just justice for my children, but for all those killed during the time of Rodrigo Duterte. I hope the killings stop for the next generation," she said, according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/families-slain-filipinos-seek-justice-dutertes-icc-trial-set-start-2026-11-27/). The rights group Rise Up for Life and for Rights held a send-off for the travelling families on Thursday, ahead of their departure for the Netherlands.

The trial also exposes how little justice the victims' families have found at home. Human Rights Watch said this week that Philippine authorities have failed to investigate the extrajudicial killings since Duterte was transferred to The Hague, despite a pledge from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to pursue prosecutions. A Justice Department task force created in November 2024 identified cases for investigation, but only four have advanced to trial, and only five cases of Duterte-era killings, involving nine police officers, have resulted in convictions. Relatives described a system in which the burden of proving an unlawful killing fell mostly on them, not on prosecutors. "It's so hard to prove that you're telling the truth," one woman whose husband was killed in a 2016 police drug sting told the organisation. Human Rights Watch also reported that drug-war abuses continue under the current administration, with police harassing, arbitrarily arresting and at times killing suspected drug dealers and users.

The proceedings will test the court itself as much as the defendant. The trial opens less than two months after the Trump administration intensified its campaign against the ICC, imposing sanctions on the institution as a whole on October 9, 2026, with sweeping financial and technological restrictions that, without protection from member states, would significantly undermine the court's ability to function. Amnesty International, which called the trial a defining test for the future of international accountability, said the proceedings demonstrate why the world must defend the court's independence. The Philippines, one of the founding members of the Rome Statute that created the court, withdrew its membership as prosecutors began investigating the drug war, which makes the trial's existence all the more remarkable.

Duterte's supporters have called for his release, and his daughter Sara Duterte, who serves as Philippine vice president, issued a statement on Wednesday ahead of the trial. The political divide over the case runs through the country's highest offices: the president who ordered Duterte's arrest and surrender, Marcos Jr., now governs alongside the family of the man on trial. That tension is likely to shadow the proceedings for as long as they last.

The contrast with other countries' handling of drug crime could hardly be sharper. Just last week, Vietnam's parliament voted to abolish the death penalty for drug trafficking entirely, narrowing capital punishment to four offences in a move its government framed as a humane, gradual reform. In the Philippines, the same policy area produced a campaign of killings that prosecutors say claimed tens of thousands of lives, and a former president now facing a court in The Hague. The two countries' opposite paths through the drug question are examined in our report on [Vietnam's decision to abolish the death penalty for drug trafficking](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/vietnam-abolishes-death-penalty-drug-trafficking-november-2026).

What happens on Monday will set the tone for a trial that could run for more than a year. The plea, the opening statements and the first witnesses will show whether the court can conduct a fair, orderly trial of a former head of state while under sanctions pressure from the world's most powerful country, and whether more than 500 victims finally get the hearing they have been denied at home. For Llore Pasco, who will spend her 73rd birthday in a courtroom in The Hague, the answer cannot come soon enough. The wider question — whether international justice can reach a leader who once seemed untouchable — will be answered in the months that follow, in a case that has already become a landmark for the court and for the Philippines. The stakes extend beyond one man: the trial is also a test of whether the institutions built to hold leaders to account can still function when great powers, including those gathered at the recent [trilateral summit in Shenzhen](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19), are challenging the rules-based order they were built to uphold.
summary: Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, 81, will stand trial at the International Criminal Court in The Hague from November 30 on crimes-against-humanity charges over thousands of killings in his anti-drug campaign, in the first trial of a former Asian leader at the court.
title: Duterte goes on trial at the ICC on Monday as families of drug-war victims seek justice
